text: They held SpaceX options for years. Then IPO talk started.
A hypothetical: 10,000 options, $2 million on paper.
An ISO lets you buy shares at a fixed strike. Here, $10.
The share value climbed to a hypothetical $210.
The gap is the spread: 10,000 x $200, or $2 million.
With an IPO in view, there are two roads out.
Disqualified: sell early, pay ordinary income rates.
Qualified: hold 2 years from grant, 1 from exercise. Long-term capital gains.
So everyone wants to exercise everything now.
But exercising counts the whole spread as income for the alternative minimum tax.
Here, an AMT bill of roughly $570,000.
Tax due in cash. Stock you can't sell yet.
The AMT returns as a credit, only when regular tax exceeds tentative minimum tax.
Here, roughly $18,000 a year, absent a sale.
If the stock falls, you paid tax on gains that never showed up.
The answer sits between all and nothing: an intersection point.
Tentative minimum tax rises with each exercise until it meets regular tax: the crossover.
Here, that is roughly 320 options a year, with about $0 of AMT.
Spread exercises across years, each sized near its crossover.
Go past it only with the credit mapped and the cash set aside.
The best tax outcome on paper can be the most expensive one in cash.
